speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: TRIBUTES ON PASSING OF FORMER U.S. SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, while it is a most unusual thing to do, the passing of John Foster Dulles, the former secretary of state of the United States, has evoked feelings of world-wide sympathy, and I shall therefore share with the house the message I sent yesterday to President Eisenhower on behalf of the parliament of Canada and the Canadian people:
May I express the deep sympathy of the government and people of Canada on the death of the Honourable John Foster Dulles.
In his passing, the American people have lost one of the outstanding figures of our time, one whose years of devoted service as secretary of state crowned a long and distinguished career in many spheres of private and public endeavour. The world has lost at a critical time a great and steadfast personality, ever vigilant in the defence of freedom.
To Canadians, he was more than a renowned world statesman: he was a friendly neighbour who regularly turned to his island home in Canada for rest and inspiration.
Our thoughts are with you and the people of the United States as you mourn the loss of one whose counsel was of such distinction and whose labours were so unstintingly given. His refusal to spare himself even when in the grip of a fatal illness will stand for years to come as an example of personal courage and public dedication.
Please extend to Mrs. Dulles and the family the expression of Canada's sorrow at his passing.
I know that the house and all Canadians will join with me in paying tribute to Mr. Dulles' memory. I may add that at the funeral in Washington on May 27 the government and people of Canada will be represented by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming).

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: TRIBUTES ON PASSING OF FORMER U.S. SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in associating our party with what the Prime Minister has just said, and particularly with his words of sympathy to Mrs. Dulles and the other members of the family, perhaps I may be permitted to read a few paragraphs from the statement I gave to the press yesterday when I heard the sad news of Mr. Dulles' death:
History will evaluate the contribution he made to the solution of international problems. But we do not need to wait for history to tell us that this contribution was a powerful, at times a decisive one, 66968-9-252J
and one that had the highest purposes behind it. His illness, and now his death, has left a vacuum in the direction of the foreign policy of his country, and indeed of the western coalition, which will not easily be filled.
He was a dedicated man and even his opponents could not but admire his courage, determination and capacity. He discharged his responsibilities with an unflagging zeal and a single-minded devotion that was beyond praise. He fought for what he believed with the intensity of a crusader and the skill of a great advocate.
He would have been a powerful and respected figure in the diplomacy and policy of any country he represented. As a spokesman of the most powerful state in the world, his was often the dominating voice. It never weakened in the pursuit, through policies in which he passionately believed, of freedom and security in the world as the foundation of peace. Those who worked with him to reach this goal, even though they may not have agreed with everything he said or did, will pay tribute to his sincerity of purpose, his clarity of mind and his magnificent courage, as they lament his passing at this time.
The free democracies have lost a great champion, whose like we shall not see again.

subtopic: TRIBUTES ON PASSING OF FORMER U.S. SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we in the C.C.F. wish to be associated with the Prime Minister and the Leader of the Opposition in sending to Mrs. Dulles, their two sons, and the members of the Dulles family our sincere sympathy at the time of the passing of John Foster Dulles. He spent his life very largely in the service of the state department of the United States. Since the time he became secretary of state ail have acclaimed his zeal, his strong will, and his complete devotion to that task.
The members of the C.C.F. movement in Canada, Mr. Speaker, have not always agreed with the policies put forward by John Foster Dulles, but we have admired his bravery throughout his life and particularly his great courage in fighting the dread disease of cancer which finally conquered him. Though we have not always agreed with his policies, we respected him as a western leader who put forward his views believing them to be right in the light of the many problems and trials confronting the world from time to time. We associate ourselves with this message of sympathy from Canada to the President of the United States and to the family.

subtopic: AGREEMENT WITH U.S. ON USE FOR MUTUAL DEFENCE

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: AGREEMENT WITH U.S. ON USE FOR MUTUAL DEFENCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to make
3966	HOUSE OF
Atomic Energy-Agreement With U.S. a statement at this time in regard to an agreement signed on May 22 in Washington between the Canadian and United States governments providing for co-operation between the two countries on the uses of atomic energy for mutual defence purposes. I trust that the house will grant me leave to make this statement. An announcement concerning this agreement is being made simultaneously in Washington. Copies of the agreement will be available in the joint parliamentary distribution branch in both languages.
This agreement will enable Canada to take advantage of the amendments made last year to the United States atomic energy act, and therefore continue and extend the degree to which co-operation in this field has been carried out under the agreement for co-operation regarding atomic information for mutual defence purposes signed in Washington on June 15, 1955, and the amendment to the civil agreement which was signed on June 26, 1956.
Under the terms of the United States act, as members of the house know, agreements for co-operation on the uses of atomic energy for mutual defence purposes must lie on the table of the joint committee on atomic energy of the United States congress for a period of 60 days after signature. It is expected, therefore, that this agreement will come into effect in approximately that period of time.
It might be helpful if I were to draw the attention of the house to the main features of this agreement, and in that connection I will use the language of the agreement. It will permit the exchange of information necessary to the development of defence plans; the training of personnel in the employment of and defence against atomic weapons and other military applications of atomic energy; the evaluation of the capabilities of potential enemies in the employment of atomic weapons; the development of delivery systems compatible with the atomic weapons which they carry; research, development and design of military reactors to the extent and by such means as may be agreed.
Provision is made for the transfer to Canada under mutually agreeable conditions of such non-nuclear parts of atomic weapons systems involving restricted data as are jointly determined to be necessary to improve the state of training of Canada's armed forces and the operational readiness of those forces. Finally, the way will be opened for the transfer at some future time to Canada of military reactors and any special nuclear materials required for them. Because of the sensitive nature of the information and materials which will be exchanged and transferred


under this agreement, certain appropriate safeguard provisions have been included.
I feel certain that the co-operation which will be carried out under this agreement will be of substantial benefit to Canada, not only in the training of our armed forces, in the development of defence plans and in the improvement in our military state of readiness and our equipment, but also in enabling Canada's armed forces better to play their part in the defence of North America and the free world.
I trust this agreement will be carried out in the same spirit which has marked the harmonious relations which have always existed between Canada and the United States on atomic energy matters.

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: AGREEMENT WITH U.S. ON USE FOR MUTUAL DEFENCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is difficult to imagine an agreement on a more important subject than the one which the Prime Minister has just read to the house. I have heard it, as have other hon. members, for the first time. I would not wish to make any comment on it without the most careful consideration. Its importance certainly warrants that consideration.
However, from what the Prime Minister has said I gather that the co-operation which is visualized between the two governments in the field of atomic weapons does not extend to the transfer of control from the United States to Canadian sources of any atomic weapons which might be manufactured in the United States and be made available to the Canadian forces for tactical or defence purposes. That, of course, is an extremely important limitation-if indeed it is a limitation-in this agreement.
As I say however, the whole matter is of such great importance that I would not wish to make any further comment on it at this time.

subtopic: AGREEMENT WITH U.S. ON USE FOR MUTUAL DEFENCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is undoubtedly one of the most important announcements that has been made in this chamber for a long time. It is most difficult, without any prior notice, to be able to state one's position immediately on such an important and complicated matter. However, the principles which guide us in looking at such documents are well known. We are interested, of course, in defence. We are interested in the protection of the integrity of Canadian sovereignty. We shall study this agreement with great care and we shall comment on it after such study in the interests of not only Canada's defence but, of even greater importance, in the interests of the peace of the world.

subtopic: JEAN ORESTE VOLCY-REPORTED STATEMENT ON REASONS FOR LEAVING CANADA

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: JEAN ORESTE VOLCY-REPORTED STATEMENT ON REASONS FOR LEAVING CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to direct a question to the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration arising out of a news report in this morning's Gazette to the effect that Mr. and Mrs. Volcy and their Canadian born daughter are now leaving Canada for the United States because, according to Mr. Volcy, they are tired of being watched by immigration officials, and that they would be permitted to remain in Canada if they were not coloured.
Would the minister care to comment on these statements and say what consideration is being given to cancellation of the deportation order so that a Canadian child will not be deprived of her birthright?

speakeroldname: Hon. Ellen L. Fairclough (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration):
subtopic: JEAN ORESTE VOLCY-REPORTED STATEMENT ON REASONS FOR LEAVING CANADA
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Assiniboia was kind enough to give me notice of his intention to ask this question and accordingly I have prepared a statement on this matter, which with the permission of the house I should like to present.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: JEAN ORESTE VOLCY-REPORTED STATEMENT ON REASONS FOR LEAVING CANADA
speechtext: I take it that the answer is somewhat longer than is usual on orders of the day?

subtopic: JEAN ORESTE VOLCY-REPORTED STATEMENT ON REASONS FOR LEAVING CANADA
speechtext: Yes, Mr. Speaker.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: JEAN ORESTE VOLCY-REPORTED STATEMENT ON REASONS FOR LEAVING CANADA

subtopic: JEAN ORESTE VOLCY-REPORTED STATEMENT ON REASONS FOR LEAVING CANADA
speechtext: Agreed.

subtopic: JEAN ORESTE VOLCY-REPORTED STATEMENT ON REASONS FOR LEAVING CANADA
speechtext:
Thank you. The facts of the case are as follows. Jean Oreste Volcy is a citizen of Haiti, 29 years of age. He entered Canada on September 6, 1951, at which time he claimed he was single and was destined to the Institut Agricole d'Oka, Quebec, to study agronomy. He remained at

that institution until the end of March, 1952, and left the institution when he failed to pass his examinations.
He registered with the school of veterinary medicine in St. Hyacinthe, Quebec in September, 1952, but again failed to pass. On July 28, 1953 he registered with the school of textiles at St. Hyacinthe, Quebec, where he obtained a diploma in cotton weaving on June 13, 1956.
On May 29, 1956 he started working for Bathurst Containers as a take-off man. At that time he declared to his employers for income tax purposes that he had three dependents, i.e. a wife, Nicole, and two children, Jean age six, and Nicole age three, all of whom he claimed were residing in Montreal.
On June 18, 1956 he registered with the Institut Alie, Montreal, for a commercial course which was due to start in September of that year. According to a letter from the Institut Alie he quit his studies there about November or December, 1956, leaving an unpaid balance of $60.
In September, 1956 he had been granted an extension of stay in Canada to expire on September 1, 1957. On September 3, 1957 Mr. Volcy called at the Montreal immigration office and requested a further extension of stay in Canada stating he was registered with the Elie business college. It was subsequently established that he had registered at the Elie business college at the beginning of September, 1957 but did not present himself when courses started on September 9, 1957, and it has been confirmed that he never attended any courses at that institution.
When he applied for an extension of his temporary stay in September, 1957, Mr. Volcy stated that he was single and requested an extension on the basis that he was still a student. He definitely claimed he would never apply for permanent admission. He also denied being employed at that time. The requested extension was granted on the basis of the information furnished, but it was subsequently established that Mr. Volcy was not then single, nor was he a student, he was employed, and in fact he later applied for permanent residence.
Upon subsequently learning that Mr. Volcy was married an effort was made to locate him at the last address furnished the immigration officials, but he had moved and his whereabouts were unknown. In November, 1957 he was located in Montreal, and when an officer of the immigration branch called to interview him a person now known to be Mrs. Volcy denied she was his wife and claimed to be only a friend.
It was established, however, that the Volcys were married in New York city in August, 66988-9-2531
Inquiries of the Ministry 1957, four months previously. Mr. Volcy further admitted that the dependents he previously claimed for income tax deduction purposes were non-existant. Mr. Volcy's attorney at this time suggested that Mr. Volcy be granted the privilege of effecting voluntary departure from Canada.
The first order of deportation was issued against Mr. Volcy in October, 1957, at which time it was not known he was married. A new order was issued in April, 1958 in which his wife, Mrs. Volcy, was included. At this time they had no children. I might say that the child has never been included in the order of deportation, and in fact remains a Canadian citizen and travels on a Canadian passport, with the right to return to Canada at any time.
When the Volcys were served with the order of deportation their solicitor argued that they had not been given an opportunity to establish that they were not subject to deportation. To meet the solicitor's objection the first order of deportation issued in April was cancelled and new orders were issued by the minister on October 28, 1958, only after a complete review of the representations made by the solicitor on behalf of his client. These deportation orders were served on the Volcys on November 10, 1958, and they were released under a conditional bond on that date.
On November 14, 1958 a petition for prohibition was served on the minister, and this was dismissed by the courts in Montreal on December 19, 1958. On January 6, 1959 the solicitor filed an appeal and deportation was accordingly suspended. In the meantime the Volcys applied for United States visas in November, 1958 and they effected voluntary departure from Canada on May 24, 1959.
From the time the deportation order was first issued until they left Canada voluntarily they were never watched by immigration officials, as has been alleged, but remained at liberty while complying with the conditions of the bond under which they were released.
This case has been given a great deal of publicity, and it has been alleged that the Volcys were being deported because of their ethnic origin. I must deny this categorically. It is well known to hon. members that Canada admits students from many lands, and of every ethnic origin, and they encounter no difficulty as long as they continue their studies. It is evident from the summary of the Volcy case, however, that from 1956, at least, Mr. Volcy has not been a bona fide student but has rather endeavoured to remain in Canada permanently by various devious means. He is not admissible as an immigrant under Canadian immigration

Inquiries of the Ministry regulations, and his record is not such as to warrant any special consideration.

Mr. Speaker, that question arose in the house on February 24 and was answered on that occasion. There must be a misunderstanding among some people in Canada with regard to this matter, or perhaps the information has not reached them through the press. The answer is that there will be two questions on the census return, one dealing with the country of citizenship, to which the answer will normally be, of course, "Canada," although those who have not their citizenship papers will reply "United Kingdom" or "United States" or whatever country of which they happen to be a citizen. There is a blank space left if the country is not named in the form. It is open to people to indicate and write in the country if it is not listed.
Then there is a second question: "What is your ethnic descent on the father's side?" There people may list their ethnic descent as they wish. The form carries about 24 types of ethnic groups, and again a blank space is left for those who do not find there the one they wish to put down. To that question people may answer "Canadian" if they so desire, or "English" or "Welsh" or "French" or "Polish" or whatever ethnic group from which they claim descent.

speechtext: The house resumed from Friday, May 22, consideration of the motion of Mr. Churchill for the second reading of Bill No. C-49 to provide for the establishment of a national energy board.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext:
The bill does introduce a new principle, recommended by the Borden commission, that no pipe line and no international power line shall be built until the board has certified as to the public convenience and necessity of the project. This, of course, is the legal way of saying that the board must consider the factor of competition and the possible injury which a proposed line might do to an existing line. After all that the Conservative party has said about encouraging competition, the introduction of legislation making "public convenience and necessity" a factor is to say the least an interesting development.
But this principle is to go hand in hand with another principle, namely control by the government; for it is clear from the bill that no new pipe line for the transmission of hydrocarbons may be built, even if its public convenience and necessity are fully established to the satisfaction of the board, unless the government gives its approval. This is an entirely new requirement, which seems to be in strange contradiction with the lofty statements made by the Prime Minister in Hull on May 7, 1957 when, according to the Ottawa Citizen of May 8, he said:
We will put a stop to the government going into business and gradually exercising control over the economy.
The bill also introduces another surprising principle. I say "surprising" because it is in direct contradiction of what was said in the house by the present Minister of Public Works (Mr. Green). If we look at page 1528 of Hansard of February 25, we can read the following words uttered by the present Minister of Public Works when he was sitting on this side of the house in 1955:
I do not suppose it would be possible to have a power of revocation much wider than the one contained in the present act. Then there is the power to limit exportation to the surplus after Canadian needs have been met, and also to regulate the price on export so that price will not be lower than the price charged to Canadian consumers.
This refers to the present requirement of the regulations adopted pursuant to the Exportation of Power and Fluids and Importation of Gas Act. Regulation 9 requires that the price for power or gas exported by a licensee shall not be lower than the price at which power or gas, respectively, is supplied by him or his supplier in similar quantities and under similar conditions of sale for consumption in Canada.
The Montreal Star of March 15, 1958, in reporting a meeting at Calgary on the previous day, said:
Mr. Dlefenbaker added, however, that his government was determined to see that gas prices charged in Canada were not used to subsidize gas sales at cheaper prices to the United States.

I may not, on second reading, quote the relevant provision of the bill, but I do point out that the act under which the present regulations were adopted is to be repealed and that the bill does no more than to require the price for export to be just and reasonable. It does not say that gas prices charged in Canada are not to be used to subsidize gas sales at cheaper prices to the United States, despite all the determination which the Prime Minister expressed when he addressed a meeting in Calgary.
The bill contains yet another principle on which I wish to comment. It is that the government proposes to arrogate to itself the power, without further reference to parliament, to control through the board the importation of oil. As to this vitally important matter, as to the reasons for asking for such far-reaching authority, such exorbitant power for the executive, all the minister could say last Monday was:
However, a section of the bill will deal with this important matter and if approved by parliament will give authority to the governor in council to extend the application of the relevant portion of the bill to oil.
These words may be found at page 3768 of Hansard of May 18. Not one word of argument, not one single reason was invoked by the minister in support of the preposterous demand for more power for the executive. What has he said on Friday which adds to the empty words he used on Monday last?
I shall close by drawing attention to the fact that repeatedly in the bill the government is asking parliament to permit it by order in council to modify the requirements of the bill, to exempt some from its application, and to adopt regulations without their nature and scope being specified.
Mr. Speaker, we have waited nearly two years for this bill. We had been led to expect some bold steps forward, but we find on reading the bill that, as the minister has said, it draws extensively upon the experience of the past. We find that the steps forward are timid and unpromising. But because the bill draws so heavily on Liberal legislation, there is a great deal in the bill to which we do not object. It fails to do much with regard to the integration of the existing agencies of the government that are concerned with energy in some form or another but I hope that when we consider the bill clause by clause we shall persuade the government that many improvements in the bill ought to be made.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising to speak on this bill which in essence sets up the machinery to organize and regulate the use and export of our
National Energy Board energy resources in Canada and also establishes a national energy board I believe I can safely say it is one of the most important pieces of legislation particularly for western Canada that has been considered by parliament for many years. It is just as important or perhaps even more important that the farm stabilization bill which considered for the first time the element of cost of production when setting floor prices.
For many years prior to the setting up of the Borden commission and since that date the people of the province of Alberta have been waiting and watching with anxiety for the implementation of a sound federal policy in reference to our national resources, natural gas and petroleum. I commend this legislation to the house as giving us that sound policy.
In particular the people of Alberta have been watching with anxiety to see what medium would be set up to consider, approve and reject applications for the building of transmission pipe lines for the transmission of gas and for the purpose of the export of natural gas, a top economic energy source produced in western Canada today which has been explored and discovered in large quantities and which exploration and discovery, I suggest, is still in its infancy.
For years in the province of Alberta the provincial Liberal party opposed the export of gas not only from Alberta to the United States but also to other parts of Canada, on two grounds. In the first place they felt there was an inadequate supply for the for-seeable future for Alberta and, secondly, that the export of natural gas to other parts of Canada and elsewhere would increase the price of natural gas to the consumer in Alberta. These objections were based on fear and lack of knowledge rather than on vision and logic.
We have only to examine the Canada Year Book of 1957-58 and refer to page 510 to determine the tremendous development that has taken place. I should like to place the following on the record:
The rapid development of Canada's petroleum and natural gas resources, initiated by the Leduc oil field discovery of 1947, continues unabated. At the end of 1956 proved reserves of crude oil and natural gas liquids totalled 3,129,304,000 barrels compared with 72 million barrels at the end of 1946 and during the intervening ten-year period, production amounted to 657,605,839 barrels. In 1956, the new oil found was more than three times the actual production which, at 170,569,200 barrels was more than 22 times the 1946 output. Natural gas reserves in 1956 were in excess of 23 trillion cubic feet compared with 4.7 trillion in 1950. Crude oil has, since 1953, maintained its lead in annual production value for all mineral produced in Canada and natural gas is entering the period of rapid growth.
May I suggest that what is set out in the Canada Year Book has been corroborated by

National Energy Board the Borden commission in the findings of that body based on ample evidence carefully examined. We now have a known and proven reserve of 23 trillion cubic feet of natural gas in Alberta and an unproven reserve estimated in the western Canada sedimentary basin of between 300 and 400 trillion cubic feet. I wish now to place on the record a statement from the report of the Borden commission:
Although the findings of the oil and gas conservation board indicate that Alberta had, as at March 31, 1958, only 4.1. trillion cubic feet of natural gas, which could be declared surplus to future requirements of the province, existing permits and immediately contractable requirements of Trans-Canada Pipe Lines Limited for Canadian market, the board estimated future discoveries to the year 1987 to be 51 trillion cubic feet. It concluded that future Canadian requirements, other than those mentioned, would be adequately protected by these future expected discoveries.
May I suggest that a very good analogy which emphasizes the weakness of the argument to keep the natural gas in Alberta for Albertans is the same type of argument that was used in the 20's in reference to the coal reserves of Alberta. This argument was used by speakers both inside this house and outside of it approximately 20 or 30 years ago. Although it was said then that Alberta had approximately 65 per cent to 75 per cent of the coal reserves of Canada, there were those who were shortsighted enough to argue that we must be careful about exporting coal to ensure that the reserves in Alberta did not become depleted; they might not be sufficient for the foreseeable needs of the people of that province and of Canada.
Today we find that a new form of energy, natural gas, has replaced coal. These 30 years have gone by, and what has happened? We were so cautious that we went to bed with our coal. Some people say coal may have a future in 20 or 30 years, but that is little comfort today to the people in Alberta who have gone bankrupt in the coal industry nr to those miners who are now unemployed. May I suggest that the time was long overdue Tor the appointment of this royal commission. The last speaker talked about delay. I say that there was delay on the part of the former government because they should have set up this commission at an earlier date and introduced the legislation that is now before us.
This bold and aggressive step taken by this government to set up the energy board, with the powers outlined in this bill, should give the people in Alberta and the rest of the prairie provinces, assurance that we shall not go to bed with the natural gas in Alberta and elsewhere as we did with coal. A sound federal policy setting up the energy board will stimulate exploration and hence
[Mr. WooUiams.l
further discovery of natural gas well beyond the imagination of those experts who made these estimates. Often estimates are only guesswork. The production of natural gas will produce untold wealth and create a new and far-reaching prosperity for western Canada, and hence Canada generally. One has only to look back on the pages of history to find that the early explorers who first set eyes on the prairie plains described them as a windswept desert and a non-productive plain. What does the record show? Over the years we have seen the prairies produce in one year from 400 million to 600 million bushels of wheat and millions of head of cattle.
What we need today is men of vision and foresight in connection with this particular form of energy, such as we had in connection with the development of the prairies for agricultural purposes. Let us not be planners filled with fear and caution with reference to the development of natural gas and with reference to the export of natural gas.
The energy board that is set up by this legislation can and should be in a position to decide expeditiously-which is always important in industry-the quantity of the surplus that can be exported in order to make use of the developed resources and turn this natural gas into wealth that can be used for further exploration and discovery. If the early pioneers had been forbidden to produce grain in such quantities on the prairies since 1900 because of the fear of wearing out the most valuable resource of all in western Canada, the topsoil, what development would have taken place in the west? The important part of this legislation is that one body, the energy board, is empowered to give permission to build transmission pipe lines and to license the export of gas. Both of these decisions are a necessary part of the marketing of the commodity.
I presume, from a reading of the bill itself, that this board will be set up similar to a court, and will examine evidence which may suggest that another pipe line should be built or that some amount of gas should be exported. Then, after this examination of the evidence, the board will exercise its discretion, subject of course to the approval of the governor in council. These decisions are a necessary part of the marketing of the commodity. This is a superior method to having two important steps controlled by two independent authorities, the board of transport commissioners and the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Churchill).
In brief, I commend this legislation to hon. members because the authority to permit the building of a pipe line and the obtaining of

an export licence are under the jurisdiction oi one body, the energy board. Under clause 27 of the bill in question-I believe I am right in saying that on second reading I am discussing the principle of the bill and I should not read the wording of the clauses of the bill-a certificate of public convenience may be granted, while under clauses 82 and 83 a licence to export gas may likewise be granted. Both of these decisions can no doubt be made at the same time and based on the same evidence. As the Minister of Trade and Commerce stated in his remarks when introducing this legislation, "This method will simplify the procedure". May I quote from his remarks when introducing this legislation? He said:
At the same time, since they must compete at the point of origin for supplies of gas and compete at the point of sale with other fuels and energy sources, there is a substantial element of risk for gas transmission companies. For this reason they must not be prevented by regulatory action from earning a return sufficient to attract capital, nor must management be deprived of the normal incentive to improve efficiency.
In these words, we see the element of flexibility in the bill. Then, the minister further stated, and I quote:
Neither in the case of oil pipe lines nor in the case of gas pipe lines will the public gain anything if regulation is so restrictive as to put the pipe lines out of business, or discourage their normal development, or impede the building of new pipe lines to serve new or expanding markets, or restrict the essential work of exploration and discovery of further reserves of oil and gas. Our objective, therefore, is to find the means and level of regulation that will adequately protect the public interest, and particularly the interest of the consumer, while maintaining healthy conditions for the pipe line industry, the oil and gas producing industries and the industries distributing oil products and gas for consumption.
This flexibility is necessary to maintain the interest, first of the industry itself so that it will continue to widen the horizon of discovery to ensure that new quantities of gas can and will be discovered. Millions of dollars have already been spent by the industry in question in exploring and discovering the reserves that we now have, and it was because of the risk that was taken and the faith that those in the industry had, that the Borden commission was able to report that there was, in fact, a surplus over and above the foreseeable future needs of Canada. As I said a while ago, 80 years ago there were those who spoke gloomily about the reserves of coal in Alberta. May I say, Mr. Speaker, that there is evidence that we went to bed with our coal, so let us hope this new legislation and this new board will make certain that we will not go to bed with the natural gas in Alberta.
We hear a lot from the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue) about full employ-
National Energy Board ment and economic prosperity. If the government had seen fit to implement the regulations suggested by the hon. member which would have strangled the industry would the men in the petroleum and natural gas industry be willing to take the risk? Would they have faith in the future of the industry itself? I remember the same type of speech was made in 1945 in Saskatchewan by Premier Douglas and the members of his government. What took place? The drilling rigs that were situated in Saskatchewan pulled out and went into the province of Alberta. This is probably one of the main reasons that we have the development in Alberta which we have today because this was at the time of the Leduc discovery.
Sometimes when one sits in his place in the House of Commons and listens to the rantings of the hon. member for Assiniboia one is reminded of those early speeches that were made by the men who promoted the Russian revolution, which finally destroyed not only economic freedom but political freedom as well. It was the same kind of talk, I suggest, that drove the industry in question out of the province of Saskatchewan. May I suggest also that that industry returned to the province of Saskatchewan only when members of that government had finally realized that there was something to the system after all, and they themselves saw that they could enrich their own pockets; and so there must have .been a place * in industry for others.
In reference to the stand which the Liberal party has taken in the province of Alberta, I should like to read from an editorial of December 11, 1957 in the Calgary Albertan, in which is discussed the Liberal stand in reference to the export of gas at that time. It reads in part as follows:
Last weekend the provincial Liberal party had a meeting of sorts in Edmonton. Naturally it had to say something about gas. But a more meaningless and cowardly statement it could not have made. The party is still obviously confused, still hopelessly ignorant of the industry and issues.
It called for a "maximum availability of natural gas for domestic and industrial users in the province, having regard to economics involved". Nobody disagrees. Nobody at all. But does the provincial Liberal party realize that the maximum local availability can only be obtained as the result of a vast and thriving export industry.
It called for a provincial gas policy which would "encourage the establishment of new industries within the province".
There again, evidence is conclusive that the maximum local industrialization will come through a policy of maximum export. If the Liberal party agrees, why it is beating around the bush?
Finally, it says "any policy of gas export from Albera shall first take into consideration the present and future interests of the province, and especially the matter of protecting the consumers of Alberta in the matter of costs".

National Energy Board.
There again there should be no doubt or hesitation. With export,-
That is to the rest of Canada.
-the price is likely to go up. Without export it is likely to go up very much higher. And besides the benefits accruing to the people from a healthy gas export industry will far more than offset any increase in price.
So, is the provincial Liberal party in favour of gas exports or is it not? If it is, why doesn't it say so? If it has the best interests of the province at heart, why doesn't it add its voice to the protests of the government?
Speaking personally, Mr. Speaker, may I say that it seems to me that natural gas is a commodity which is different from beef or wheat. It seems to me that there is a weakness in the argument, which is to keep gas in Alberta or in any other province and that it is just as weak as that which says "keep beef in the foothills of Alberta because the price will be cheaper". But where will be the prosperity of the rest of the province and of the rest of the country? The same argument would apply with regard to wheat. Hence, when I hear Liberals stand in their places and criticize this government about delay, I would remind them of what has taken place in the province of Alberta. The Borden commission should have been set up by the previous government and the energy board should have been set up by the previous government so that we could have got things going, so that there would be prosperity in the west such as we have never seen before.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is always a pleasure to listen to the remarks of the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Woolliams) inasmuch as they are so reassuring. Every time we listen to him we get a little bit more evidence of the rightness of the cause of the members of the C.C.F.
In order to deal with this bill that is before us today, Mr. Speaker, I think it would be appropriate to do a little review as to just what are the reasons why we have it before us. Bills do not come before the house just for the sake of giving us something to do. Usually there is a good reason and sometimes there is a long neglected reason before we get a bill presented to the house for its approval. I think we all realize that this bill is based, at least to a certain extent, on the report of the royal commission which was appointed on October 15, 1957 and which of course brought in the report of October 1958.
If we go back a little further I think we will realize that the royal commission was set up as a result of the Trans-Canada pipe line debate which almost rocked this house on its very foundations. In fact, I

think we could pin it down even closer than that if we refer to the remarks of the former hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar when he spoke in this house during the 1957-58 session. At that time he referred to the remarks made by the former leader of the Conservative party. In connection with this particular bill which is before us now I think it might be an appropriate time to put those words on record again. These are his words as found at page 4673 of Hansard of June 4, 1956:
*-enlarge the powers of the crown corporation so that the entire pipe line may be constructed immediately under public ownership.
Mr. Speaker, all this has led up to the report of the royal commission of last year. But what has happened to the important recommendations contained in that report? In this bill which is before us today what is there that enables this board to deal with the famous Texas buccaneers, to use the words of our present Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker)? What indeed is contained in this bill to deal with the Ontario buccaneers who had improved even on the Texas buccaneers, and go right up to cabinet rank in their government? Where are the safeguards that are going to give protection to the people of this country in the future where they did not have protection in the past? We find some of these recommendations in the report of the commission but we do not find any in this bill. For a moment I should like to give one or two examples. If we turn to page XII of the royal commission report, recommendation 21, paragraph (b), we find these words:
(ii) The financial structure, ownership, financing, engineering and construction plans of any applicant and the opportunity for the people of Canada to participate in the financing, engineering and construction of the project.
I think those are significant words. I should like to draw particular attention to the words "and the opportunity for the people of Canada to participate in the financing". I should now like to turn to the bill that is before us in order to see how this particular phase appears in that bill. In clause 44, paragraph (d) we find these words:
(d) the financial responsibility and financial structure of the applicant, the methods of financing the line and the extent to which Canadians will have an opportunity of participating in the financing, engineering and construction of the line;
There is quite a difference in the phraseology or the wording of those two otherwise approximately similar sections. I do not know, of course, what the purpose of the commission was when they worded this particular recommendation as they did. However, I would go this far. I would say that

there is a reasonable doubt that they possibly came as close as the people sitting on this commission could come, when you realize their responsibilities, their duties and their position, to recommending that the trans-Canada pipe line and other similar projects should be public utilities in this country. I cannot see any reason why this particular clause should be worded as it is. There is certainly no hint given in the words of the clause of the bill. There is no room for doubt there; any doubt in regard to the recommendations of the royal commission has been very carefully left out.
Now I would like to come to another point. If we look at the report, on page IX we find recommendation 12, which has been mentioned before during this debate. It reads:
That the prices, tolls, rates or tariffs of a company owning or operating an oil or gas pipe line, as regulated by the board of transport commissioners for Canada, should be just and reasonable, non-discriminatory and calculated to yield a fair rate of return on the shareholders' equity, after making due allowance for reasonable and proper operating expenses, depreciation, interest, income and other taxes.
We find a section in the act which deals with the same subject, clause 52, entitled "Tolls to be just and reasonable". That clause reads as follows:
All tolls shall be just and reasonable, and shall always, under substantially similar circumstances and conditions with respect to all traffic of the same description carried over the same route, be charged equally to all persons at the same rate.
Once again, Mr. Speaker, we find that the very important and pertinent words "on the shareholders' equity" have been very carefully left out of this bill. I think this is very significant, Mr. Speaker. When we think back to the famous or infamous debate on the Trans-Canada pipe line and think of the ringing words of the present Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) spoken in this very house about these Texas buccaneers, and so on and so forth, we must remember that at this time there was supposition on his part. We had not experienced their actual operations in this country; we had not seen just what these people would do. That no longer is so. We have had many opportunities to view just what these buccaneers have done, both the foreign and the domestic buccaneers.
I think possibly the actions we have seen over the past two or three years may have greatly influenced those recommendations which were brought down by this royal commission. But what has happened? In spite of the fact that the royal commission made the recommendations, this present government is still unwilling or unable to act in the interests of the Canadian people. Once
National Energy Board more if we look back at the bill, on page 18 we find clause 62, which deals with the general powers of the board. I am not going to read all of these different subclauses to clause 62, but it does raise another matter of which we have had ample experience in this country, and that is the question of the abuse that can be made of the law. As I understand it, this clause has been transferred almost word for word, if not word for word, from other legislation which was previously on the books of this country.
It is true that according to the law some of the practices which have been carried on by these various pipe line companies were actually outside the law. But there was no provision in the legislation to uphold the law, and consequently it was left to each poor individual little farmer, or whoever was involved, to hire expensive legal aid and to go through very expensive court action in order to uphold the law. I do not want to list at great length some of the practices to which I am referring. I would just like to refer hon. members to speeches made by the hon. member for Timiskaming (Mr. Peters) and myself, found on pages 1183 and 1185 of Hansard for June 16, 1958. Hon. members will find many of them listed there, and they are some of the actions with which we are very familiar because they happened as the pipe line was going through my constituency. The only ones I would like to add today are ones which have been brought to my attention since the completion of that line.
As one reads the clause one finds that these companies are responsible for any damage done. They are responsible to leave the ground as they find it, and all that sort of thing. Unfortunately that is not the case. I could take hon. members to many places and many farms throughout my riding and throughout the riding of Timiskaming where great damage was done. Fences were not put back up again, fields were not graded. In one particular case a farmer's wood lot was expropriated and they cut a strip 200 feet wide, changed their minds and moved to another place where they cut another 200-foot strip through the farmer's wood lot, changed their minds again and went back to the first lot and left his property in that condition, and when he asked about damages they said he could go ahead and sue.
We have seen cases very recently of how much it costs to uphold the law of this country. I think an excellent example is the Roncarelli case in the province of Quebec where it cost, I think, something in the neighbourhood of $35,000 to uphold the law. I think the government has a duty to the people of this country to protect the small farmer and

National Energy Board other people who are involved who cannot afford costly law suits in order to uphold the law of the country.
Mr. Speaker, in the limited experience we have had I think it has been well demonstrated over the years that the best defence that the Canadian people can have in matters of this kind is that of public ownership of these utilities. At least when we have public ownership it is under the responsibility of the government, and the government is responsible to the people. Certainly these companies are not responsible to anyone but themselves. As has been demonstrated in many cases, they are not even responsible to the law unless one can afford to uphold the law. It is also quite apparent from this bill that the government has no intention of setting up anything, except what might be described as a Punch and Judy show as far as this board is concerned. I am sure the board will be out front dancing while the government is behind pulling the strings, because from what I can see of this bill that is all the board will be entrusted with.
If we look at the report of the royal commission, recommendation No. 23 on page XIII reads as follows:
That the enabling legislation contain provisions to ensure the independence of the members of the board.
When we pick up this bill we find clause after clause after clause is always subject to the approval of the governor in council. How can this board have any independence if every move it makes is subject to the approval of the governor in council? How can this board take any action against these pirates, either foreign or domestic, if it has to turn to the government every time for approval? Who knows, by this time these pirates may be just as good friends of this government as they were of the previous government. I maintain that the bill to set up this board is not doing the job which the people of this country expected. I maintain it is not doing the job that it should do. In fact, it would appear to me that this government is hiding behind this sham board which is being set up to take any blame that might be levelled at its policy, though, in reality, the board is obliged to do the government's bidding.
With this in mind, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam (Mr. Regier):
That this bill be not read a second time until further consideration has been given to the public ownership of interprovincial gas and oil pipe lines.

speechtext:
I rise with a great deal of pleasure to speak on this energy bill because, like many hon. members in this house, I feel that the principle of the establishment of a national energy board is one which should have been adopted long ago.
I felt some concern listening to the hon. member for Villeneuve (Mr. Dumas) the other day when he indicated that the national Liberal convention of 1958 had advocated the setting up of a national energy board. I think that at that time-and today, too-we would accuse him and his colleagues of "me tooism", because up to that date they had not indicated any intention of considering the establishment of a national energy board or of a national energy plan.
I wish to confine my remarks today to the oil and gas industry, as this represents a most urgent question. It is true that coal is a form of energy which presents a serious problem, but I suggest that this is a matter of somewhat longer range. We in Alberta have great quantities of coal, and regardless of the remarks which were made by the hon. member for Gloucester (Mr. Robichaud) the other day, coal is certainly going to be studied by the Borden commission. Surely one cannot expect the commission to look into every facet of energy within its terms of reference before writing a report; in other words, surely he does not expect we should have to wait for the whole study to be completed before we could consider those immediate aspects which are of particular importance to us today.
The oil and gas industry is a very young and virile industry. It made its debut on a commercial basis in 1920, but one could go back a good deal earlier in history as far as Ontario is concerned, though production was on no very great scale. Our oil and gas industry in this country really dates from February, 1947 with the discovery of Leduc No. 1. Today it has advanced to its present position, I would suggest, under the stimulus of several factors; first, a greatly expanding domestic and foreign market; second, the Middle East crisis of 1955-56, which created a scarcity of petroleum products on the North American continent and, third, the methods of development by reason of the very nature of oil and gas, and also because of the land policy adopted in this country which encourages development. There have been many criticisms of this policy.
Let us look at the progress the oil and gas industry has made. First of all, it has climbed in the short space of 12 years into the No. 1 spot among Canada's mineral producing industries, in terms of capital investment, employment created and value of

production. Second, oil refining capacity-in Canada has been trebled to a current 800,000 barrels daily, an expansion which has kept pace with the near tripling in 12 years of Canada's petroleum consumption. Third, another indication of growth is that oil productive capacity, only 20,000 barrels daily 12 years ago, has increased over fifty fold to a current potential exceeding one million barrels a day. Fourth, oil markets climbed from 20,000 barrels daily in early 1947 to over half a million barrels daily in
1957.	They slumped to some 460,000 barrels in 1958 due to reduced export demand, but they began 1959 at well above half a million barrels daily, still only about 54 per cent of potential. Canada's production now equals about two-thirds of Canada's consumption, although the nation's productive capacity makes self-sufficiency either in fact or in balance quite feasible.
Proven reserves of crude oil and other liquid petroleums, which were under 100 million barrels at the beginning of 1947, climbed to about 3.6 billion barrels by the end of 1958, despite production of some one billion barrels in the 12-year period. In
1958,	for each one barrel produced, more than three barrels of reserves were discovered.
Proved reserves of natural gas, which were about 1.5 trillion cubic feet at beginning of 1947, climbed to about 28.5 trillion cubic feet by the end of 1958 despite production of 1.8 trillion cubic feet in the 12-year period. In 1958, despite record production of about 400 billion cubic feet, almost ten cubic feet of reserves were discovered for each one cubic foot consumed.
A recent summary published by the Alberta government indicates that in the period between 1947 and the end of 1958 there have been drilled in Alberta 9,121 oil wells, 1,335 gas wells and 3,975 dry wells. Remember that last figure: it represents a tremendous loss in investment. Taking into account the adjustments from 1959 to date, recent figures indicate that there are some 8,800 producing wells in Alberta and some 3,850 in Saskatchewan. In Alberta there are some 700 producing gas wells and about 870 capped gas wells. These capped wells represent a tied up investment of close to $200 million from which no one is drawing any benefit. In that period of time, 1947 to 1958, some $2,800 million was spent on exploration and development, and in the last three years money was spent at a rate in excess of $360 million per annum. That is an indication, Mr. Speaker, of the investment that has been made not only by Canadians but by people
National Energy Board foreign to this land in our oil and gas industry in the short space of 12 years.
What has that industry meant to Alberta? It has meant the employment of upwards of 150,000 people who in some way or other derive all or part of their livelihood from exploration, development and production and marketing of oil. Second, we have had a multi-million dollar petrochemical industry established in that area. Third, we have a steel industry, a pipe mill and fabricators. We had indications just the other day that one of our eastern Canadian firms plans to establish a new $10 million mill to produce up to 42-inch pipe, in the largest diameter to be produced in this country. Fourth, the revenues to the province of Alberta from the sale of crown reserves and leases, lease rentals and royalties amounted to the sum of $855,490,000 from the first of January 1947, to March 31, 1959. We have seen tremendous years such as 1956 and 1957. Nineteen hundred and fifty-eight saw a decline because of the incursion of imports into the North American market and the so-called voluntary curbs by the United States refineries and some decline of business activity. The first quarter of 1959 has seen a pickup. The rate this year is higher than 1958 but it is still only 75 per cent of the rate of 1956 and 1957.
The industry in Alberta last week produced about 319,000 barrels a day, which is only 40 per cent of the rated capacity. With these figures, I believe I can underline the seriousness of the problem of oil production and marketing. Recently there was a lifting of the compulsory quotas imposed by the United States. What has been the result? First of all there was an increase in the nominations from the Puget sound refineries to about 55,000 barrels a day, as announced this week by the nominations from those refineries to the Alberta gas conservation board. As the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Churchill) indicated the other day, the situation must be watched carefully. We must always remember that the United States refineries may choose United States domestic oil or Canadian crude oil and, therefore, the fact that those restrictions were lifted does not necessarily mean that an extra barrel of Canadian oil need be sold. However, we see that some is being sold.
Although it has been said that while the removal of restrictions may not mean an immediate increase-and I have indicated that there had been a slight, hopeful one in Canadian production-over the longer term this action will encourage an increase in the movement of Canadian oil into the natural and economic export markets of the United States.

National Energy Board
I would like to extend my congratulations to the government on the energetic steps it took to have the mandatory controls removed. I am sure that the people of Alberta and Saskatchewan-in fact the people of the whole country-will be gratified to know just how much encouragement and attention were given to this problem by their own individual members. However, removal of those quota restrictions in the United States does not increase the market for western crude in eastern Canada. In fact, the reverse may be the result, because it may serve to make competition more acute as the result of a diversion of more fire-sale crude into the eastern Canadian market. Mr. Speaker, eastern Canada must not become a dumping ground for foreign crude at the expense of domestic crude. The situation must be watched very carefully and ultimately drastic measures may be necessary. This is why I would support provisions in the act which permit the imposition of controls on oil imports or exports by proclamation when the situation may demand it.
We have just heard this afternoon, and on previous occasions, criticisms by the Liberal opposition to the effect that this gives wide and sweeping controls; it is an abdication of control by parliament. But, Mr. Speaker, surely those hon. gentlemen do not think that if the situation did boil up in the oil industry, and it could do so very quickly, we should have to wait for the summoning of another session of parliament to amend the act to bring those provisions into effect. It has been argued that it has made the position of the Borden commission impossible. But surely the situation is that the Borden commission will make its recommendations in connection with oil matters. Without binding itself in any specific way, the government has now made an open ruling. It may adopt the recommendations, not only of the Borden commission, but from other sources for dealing with the problem when it arises. I cannot see why there should be this criticism.
I can conceive, for example, of a situation arising. Last March there were price cuts in the pipe line rate of from 5 to 12 cents a barrel, and posted purchase prices for light crude were dropped from 14 to 17 cents a barrel. This meant an over-all price cut of between 19 and 29 cents a barrel in eastern Canada. What it really meant was a reduction of $25 million to the producers in western Canada. But no sooner was that cut introduced than we saw a matching reduction in the price of off-shore crude, so that the net result of the reduction was absorbed by the oil producers of western Canada.
We must also study, and with some concern, the effect of the potential movement of off-shore crude by tanker through the St. Lawrence seaway, which at the moment cannot be assessed.
People, including the premier of Alberta, have tried to lay the blame for the present situation with respect to the marketing of oil at the door of this administration. As pointed out by the Minister of Trade and Commerce the other day, quotas on imports and so forth which might be imposed by the Canadian government could have many serious short range implications; indeed, it could very seriously complicate our foreign trade position. I do not say it necessarily will but there are warning signs. We can see the warning that there are difficulties ahead. Unless the position drastically worsens, it would not appear that quotas are the immediate answer.
A suggestion has been made by certain people, including the premier of Alberta, that the federal government should call together the major companies to allocate to their eastern refineries more western crude. This proposal could be considered but I am just wondering whether the premier of my own province has done anything in this regard. After all, his contacts with the oil company have been constant and repeated over the years and one would assume that he would have some influence with these companies. I wonder what would be his government's constructive contribution to the solution of the oil marketing problem.
May we now return to the field of natural gas. Like all Albertans I look forward to an early decision on the export of this form of energy and I am sure the government is moving toward this goal. I would, however, urge upon the government to not lose sight of the fact that the passage of months before a decision is reached on export could result in the loss of an entire year from the point of view of the industry. I need not point out in detail to the house the implications of delay on employment in the pipe line construction industry and on the oil well supply firms, on our steel mills and our fabricator mills. The oil industry is marking time. It is upon this background of which I am sure the government is aware that we are making progress toward a decision.
On the other hand I find somewhat morally dishonest any statement that there have been unjustifiable and unnecessary delays in considering applications, let us say, of West Coast Transmission and Alberta and Southern Gas. After all, if we look at the record, the Alberta conservation board made its report on the application of these two companies

on March 18 last and the government decision authorizing export was made on April 7 last. No sooner had that decision been made than we heard allegations from certain government sources in the province of Alberta that it was all due to the delay of the federal government that we did not have immediate export of natural gas.
The answer to that criticism, if indeed it can be deemed a criticism, is this. Even if it had the machinery in existence, how could this administration consider a hypothetical question? It must be remembered that the export of natural gas is a two-phase operation. First of all we must consider export in excess of the needs of a province. This must be determined. We have the decisions in the case of the Alberta gas conservation board. Second, we have to consider the needs of Canada as a whole to determine whether there will be export from this country.
I am not going to speak on the application of Trans-Canada Pipe Lines Limited which is now before this administration or on the new application now before the Alberta gas conservation board. It would appear to me, however, that Trans-Canada may now be shifting its feet since its appearance before the Borden commission. It now wants a further 420 billion cubic feet over 22 years so as to export 200 million cubic feet a day through Emerson. It would now appear that if the company is to fulfil its export quota it would have to use some of its Canadian allotment over the next few years.
It is not my intention this afternoon to go into detail in outlining the differences between the principles of the bill and the recommendations of the Borden commission. Other speakers dealt with this at considerable length the other day, particularly the Minister of Trade and Commerce and the hon. member for Calgary South (Mr. Smith).
My own opinion of the speech of the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue) is that he has not read the bill or if he has read it he certainly does not understand it. I would have thought that clause 44 was a full answer to his remarks saving those which were of a strictly doctrinaire, partisan nature. The people of Canada have given their opinion as to the value they place on such remarks and the people who espouse them.
I should like to endorse the remarks made by the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Woolliams) about the change in attitude in Saskatchewan when they first approached the problem of oil and gas. Oh yes, we had all sorts of comments like those put forward by hon. members in the far left corner about controls but the net result was that there
National Energy Board was drilling and no activity for years until the Saskatchewan government saw the light and acted just a little more favourably. They have now gone a long way from their original position, but that is not the position hon. members of the C.C.F. take in this house today.
As far as the Liberals are concerned, it would be interesting to see what has been their attitude on gas. In 1951-52 they were unalterably opposed to the export of gas not only from Canada-why, they would not even consider that point-but from the province of Alberta. Then last year during the course of the election campaign I seem to recall that the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) at some meetings in Saskatchewan promised to grant a permit to Trans-Canada Pipe Lines Limited for the immediate export of gas; but at the same time his provincial colleagues were introducing a motion in the legislature of Alberta which would have required specific reference to the provincial legislature for the granting of any new export permit or the increase of any existing permit. In other words, they were going to take the powers away from the Alberta gas conservation board and so we had the two of them going by divergent paths. This illustrates that the Liberal attitude on oil and gas has not been consistent over the years.
In so far as the Conservative party in Alberta is concerned it has consistently been in favour of the export of gas under appropriate conditions. As far back as 1952 it advocated the greatest possible participation by Canada in the financing of oil and gas pipe lines. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, if I rise to take part in this debate on second reading of Bill No. C-49, which is to establish a new board known as an energy board in our country, it is not because I feel I have the technical knowledge to discuss the objects and principles of the bill. However, I am pleased to state these objects and principles were well put before the house by the hon. member for Villeneuve (Mr. Dumas) last Friday afternoon. However, there are certain principles which I feel, as the representative of Nickel Belt, I should like to discuss because, as many hon. members have said, this bill is of great interest to the people of Canada, and possibly of even greater interest to the people of northern Ontario. It is in this area that these various forms of energy are of extreme importance in the development of industry.
The purpose of this bill is to establish a commission or board which, in the interests of the Canadian people, will be asked to regulate the construction and operation of oil and gas pipe lines, and to make regulations with respect to tolls, the export and import of gas and also the export of hydro. However, it is also of interest to note that the board is to study and review, on behalf of the people of Canada all matters pertaining to forms of energy which come within the jurisdiction of the parliament of Canada. It is in this regard that the proper constitution of this new board becomes of importance.
There are, however, many indications of contradictions between the principles of the bill and the opinions expressed by members of the government. The Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Churchill) will agree that even the statement he made in introducing this bill had to be explained to this house and the people of Canada because it had been misconstrued. Everyone in Canada is familiar with the pipe line debate. This debate takes on an added significance now because we see the people who at that time made such strong protests against the expansion and transportation of the gas industry in Canada now bearing the responsibility for creating a new board which necessarily will regulate the transportation of gas.
Furthermore, I may say that the members of the Conservative party who have, on occasion, obstructed the expansion and transportation of gas in Canada now find their names linked in my province with profit making in the construction of the gas pipe

line. Of course, this bill will introduce into the development of forms of energy certain regulations but, as we all know, as society grows in Canada and elsewhere a certain amount of regulation is required. I agree with this. I am a great believer in the principle in medio stat virtus. There is no doubt that if we do have to have regulations, they must necessarily be just and proper under the circumstances. There would be great danger in Canada in either going too far, or having no regulations at all.
In this connection, I should like to place on the record the words of Mr. Askew, in his submission on behalf of the Sun Oil Company to the Borden commission, concerning this problem of infringing upon the liberty of people who try to better the development of industries in which they are interested. Mr. Askew had this to say as reported in the bulletin of the Sun Oil Company. He said:
The flight from this philosophy has been characterized by a growing effort to place the planning of the economic affairs of men in the hands of government, and increasingly to substitute rule by agencies, bureaux and boards for rule by law. The process continues, despite repeated evidence from history, extending from the days of Confucius to modern times, that rather than contribute to the material well-being of the people, it tends to dull and eventually to snuff out the very inventiveness, ingenuity and enterprise upon which economic progress is based.
It is upon these considerations that we urge a long, hard look at the proposed national energy board and the functions and authorities to be assigned to it. No matter how innocuous may their charter seem, such agencies have been shown by history to yield to irresistible pressures to extend their activities, compound their regulations, and confuse those over whom they have jurisdiction. They tend to become foci for every unrest, and soon are engaged less in protecting the people than in equalizing competitive capabilities. In this process they negate inherent economic advantage and deny its benefit to people.
I realize, of course, that although regulations are necessary, they must follow a proper and just norm and not be subjected to political pressures which in this bill I feel are seen necessarily to crop up. In this bill which brings about in Canada such an important innovation as this new board to regulate energy, the first principle which should apply is that the members of parliament should be given the proper information on which to make that decision for the Canadian people whom they represent. The Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) before the elections had a great deal to say on this matter of an energy board. I should like to quote for the benefit of the house, his remarks in 1957, namely on February 4, when he was speaking at the annual dinner of the Toronto board of trade. That is nearly two and one-half years ago. The Prime Minister then had this to say:
National Energy Board
There is a need now for the setting up of a Canadian national energy board, with its membership composed of technical personnel, who might be selected by the president of the national research council of business organizations, of the dominion and provincial governments, to the end that the most effective use of the energy resources of Canada, in the interests of the public welfare, may be assured. We have vast resources of gas and oil and coal and uranium. I believe the time has come to set up such a board, whose duty it would be to advise and to recommend proposals regarding these resources-
Mr. Speaker, this is over two and one-half years ago. I feel there is something which is not readily understood, namely why this government had to wait for those two and one-half years, especially in the light of its conduct in the last few days when, extremely swiftly, it has presented this difficult bill, as mentioned by many hon. members. This bill, consisting of 101 sections and 28 pages, as was stated, is placed before the house for a decision in this abrupt manner although the government has stated this was an emergency matter over two and one-half years ago.
In addition, members of this parliament were not furnished with certain reports and studies which necessarily were made for the preparation of this new law which we are now discussing. On that score, Mr Speaker, I should like to refer to the report of the department of the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Churchill) as far back as the year 1957. I am reading from the annual report of the Department of Trade and Commerce for 1957, at page 54, where the minister indicated that they had formed what he called the energy studies branch of his department:
The main functions of the branch are to develop systematic records and analyses relating to energy matters; to prepare studies on current energy problems requiring policy decisions in this and other departments and agencies; and to provide information and assistance to the numerous departments and agencies which are concerned with one or more aspects of energy matters.
Later on at page 55 we read the following:
It was occupied, during 1957, with studies on such questions as those relating to natural gas pipe line development, export policy for natural gas, policy relating to supervision of transmission rates and sale prices for natural gas, policy on thermal electric power developments, the effect of United States oil import restrictions on the Canadian petroleum industry, and United States proceedings related to the importation of Canadian natural gas.
Later on the same subject of energy we read the following:
Most of the study papers prepared during the period have necessarily been confidential.
Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Trade and Commerce is possibly the person from whom it is most difficult to obtain information by way of reports placed before the house. Since he has made reference in his own

National Energy Board report to these studies and reports I feel that it would have been necessary that he allow the members of parliament, the representatives of the Canadian people whose interests we are trying to protect in the matter of energy in Canada, to have that knowledge before the study and the passing of this extremely important bill.
We find something further on that score, speaking on this matter of the interests of the public and the contention that the public should be informed. We find something similar which again illustrates the conduct of the Minister of Trade and Commerce as to what is done with reports and studies which should be made available to the representatives of the Canadian people, the members of parliament.

speechtext: What accusation are you making as to what I have done with regard to reports? Do you mind repeating it?
