subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member who has just taken his seat may be surprised to learn that I am speaking on this bill without any embarrassment whatever. The fact that I am the fourth member of our party in the house to speak also shows that we are not, as a party, embarrassed in discussing this bill.
66968-9-254
National Energy Board
Now, Mr. Speaker, this is an important bill dealing with the subject of energy resources which is as important for the development of this country as any subject can be. We are debating this matter today, May 25, 1959, and it is a long time since February 4, 1957 when the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) in Toronto-these words have already been put on the record in this debate-said that the need was now for setting up a Canadian national energy board, and that the time had come to establish such a board. Four days after that statement, he said the same thing in the House of Commons.
The Prime Minister had his opportunity when the House of Commons met in October, 1957, and he was the head of the government. There was no mention in the speech from the throne at that time of the establishment of an energy board. Indeed, on October 15, I think it was, three days after the speech from the throne, the Prime Minister announced, not an energy board but a royal commission to look into the matter and to make recommendations. This royal commission, Mr. Speaker, put this whole question into a deep freeze for 19 months, for obvious reasons, and during that time I think I am right in saying that nothing was heard in this parliament about government policies dealing with this vital matter of energy resources, and national development as affected by energy resources. This is in contrast, Mr. Speaker, to what we heard on the subject from so many members of the government in earlier years when they were sitting on this side of the house.
On March 14, 1958, during the election campaign, the Prime Minister did tell the country in Calgary, in words that have also been put on the record, that the government would act immediately after the interim report of the Borden commission. This word "immediately" is now so often used by the government in statements about what it is going to do that the particular coinage has become debased, in fact there were more than six months between the interim report of this commission and the resolution dealing with the energy board which was put on the order paper on April 23 of this year. The resolution was in very general terms, and did not give us much opportunity to speculate on the type of bill that would be based on it.
The bill itself was discussed a month or so, almost a month, after the resolution was first introduced. Then, Mr. Speaker, as you know, within 24 hours of the receipt of the bill or the tabling of the bill, we were to be asked to take decisions with regard to it. That period was later extended by a day or so. It was a period which would not have

National Energy Board given members on this side of the house the opportunity to which they were entitled to make a real study and analysis of the bill and would not have given an opportunity for the expression of views by interests concerned in the country with this important matter.
Of course, Mr. Speaker, we naturally wondered why, after such a long delay, there should have been so much haste. As was stated this afternoon by my friend the hon. member for Lapointe (Mr. Brassard), I think it was, this is another example of inept handling on the part of the government of an extremely important piece of legislation. Here we have had long delay, without any discussion or without any information on the matter, folowed by a sudden, ill-considered burst of speed in order to make up for the loss of time, by the introduction of legislation which was to be decided without any delay. We are becoming familiar with that particular pattern of activity in this house.
I suggest, as other hon. members on this side of the house have already suggested, that that delay was quite unnecessary. Surely it is now clear.-as indeed we on this side of the house stated would be the case at that time -that the appointment of the Borden commission was merely an unnecessary delaying tactic, and that it was not necessary for that commission to go into this matter as it is still going into it in order for the government to have made up its mind as to what it wished to do. As a matter of fact, the proof of that contention is that the government is now largely by-passing-as so many hon. members have pointed out-the first report of the commission, while the legislation which is now before us has been introduced before the second report of the commission has even been submitted. The commission, however, has accomplished its purpose in providing an extremely useful delaying tactic for the government at a price, as was pointed out last Friday, of some $300,000 or more.
In his statement last Friday the minister admits that the major part of this bill before us comes almost textually from the Pipe Lines Act and from the Exportation of Power and Fluids and Importation of Gas Act and that most of the other provisions that are not textually from those two acts, including the creation of a national energy board, were recommended in the Gordon Commission report. That report, which was in the hands of the government in 1957 and which included a special study of this question of gas and oil, surely provided the government with

sufficient information on which it could have acted if it had desired to do so, especially as the present bill now before us has in effect repudiated the major recommendations of the commission which followed the Gordon report.
This particular bill is an even more drastic repudiation of all the feverish words and emotional arguments put forward by the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) and his colleagues, including the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Churchill), during the pipe line and earlier debates on this general subject of energy. The present bill contains no provision to realize the Prime Minister's vision of Canadian resources development by Canadians. It contains no safeguards, so often clamoured for and even recommended as desirable in the Borden report itself, to ensure the maximum possible Canadian ownership and control of resources development. It contains no provisions to encourage the processing of raw materials in Canada-that was another strong Conservative battle cry when in the opposition 

through effective utilization for that purpose of our great sources of energy in this country; and I hope to have a word to say about that matter later. It contains no provisions-and we have heard a great deal about this matter also-for keeping Texas or other buccaneers out of our affairs or limiting the extremely exorbitant profits about which the Prime Minister and the minister used to get so indignant.
In this bill, Mr. Speaker, you will find nothing dealing with these matters. That which is contained in this bill could surely have been brought in, if the government had so desired, in October 1957. Had it been brought in then, time and money would have been saved and many months of uncertainty and confusion about government policy would have been avoided, which uncertainty and confusion, as the hon. member for Calgary South (Mr. Smith) pointed out over a year ago, were bound to have an unsettling effect on the industries and areas most concerned.
As to the bill itself, may I say this. The hon. member for Calgary South, speaking at the resolution stage of the bill on May 18, had this to say as reported at page 3779 of Hansard:
I can appreciate, as can most hon. members, the difficulty of the government in attempting to reconcile the two extreme views which have been expressed in relation to the Bordon royal commission, namely those on the one hand who have stated their belief that the industry should not be in any way restricted by regulation, and those on the other hand who believe that a tight form of legislation is required in the interests of Canadian consumers.

And the hon. member went on to say this:
It is my contention that it is not inconsistent to believe-
Whatever that may mean.
-that there can be introduced into and be passed by parliament a bill which, to a substantial degree, will satisfy both of these two extremes.
In other words, Mr. Speaker, according to the hon. member for Calgary South this is the kind of bill which will satisfy those on the one extreme who do not want any regulation at all and those on the other extreme who want a tight and complete regulation, as he put it. That is a fairly impossible objective for any piece of legislation, namely to satisfy both extremes and I do not think it is met by the bill that we have before us.
So far as the principle of the bill is concerned may I say this. As has already been stated-and I am happy to repeat it-the broad principle of this bill is satisfactory to this party. Of course, it should be satisfactory because in January, 1958 our party put itself on record in favour of a national energy authority. We therefore accept that principle because we stand by our platform. But as has already been pointed out, that does not mean that we support all the provisions of this bill or that we believe that this bill is adequate to implement the principle we support. On the contrary, we feel that this bill -and we shall try to point this out in more detail when we get to the committee stage- contains many sins of omission and commission.
Let me look for a moment at one extremely important function mentioned in the bill, that of research and investigation by the board. The administrative duties of the board which are proposed in this bill are limited by the bill itself to oil, gas and international power lines. But the functions of research and investigation and of report and recommendation are absolutely unlimited. They cover the whole field of energy, as I understand it, without any limitation whatever. Furthermore, clause 22 of the bill does not say that the board "may" study these matters. That particular clause says that the board "shall" study these matters. Hence we ask ourselves why there is this difference in the scope of the two main functions which are allocated by the bill to the board. This question becomes of special importance, because, as has already been pointed out, there are other agencies of government at this time which have research and advisory functions in the energy field which are not touched by this legislation. Obviously there arises the danger of duplication, with its resulting confusions, conflicts and waste. When the minister was discussing the resolution, long before we had the chance 66968-9-2541
National Energy Board of seeing the bill, the minister said-I am paraphrasing what he said-that the major purpose of this bill was to consolidate, to coordinate, to pull together governmental functions in this field. On Monday, May 18, as reported at page 3766 of Hansard, the minister said that this legislation was in fulfilment of a long held objective of his party to bring this about, and to support that view he quoted a statement which the present Minister of Public Works (Mr. Green) made on February 25,	1955, at page 1530 of
Hansard for that year. This is the quotation of the Minister of Public Works put on record with much approval by the present Minister of Trade and Commerce. The former member for Vancouver Quadra said:
We believe there is a great need for an over-all energy policy. Let us get away from dealing with the problem piecemeal with different departments concerned. It is not an efficient way to deal with these important matters.
That is what the Minister of Trade and Commerce quoted the present Minister of Public Works as saying in 1955, and he quoted him with approval. But the minister who introduced the bill did not remain convinced for very long of the validity of the argument of the Minister of Public Works, because on second reading last Friday the Minister of Trade and Commerce told us that all the existing agencies were to be left unchanged. Quoting from his statement last Friday, he said, as reported on page 3930 of Hansard:
While the board's advisory functions require that it be free to study any aspect of energy, we do not believe it would be profitable under present circumstances to disrupt the existing agencies involved in these related fields.
We know what these agencies are because they have been put on the record, but perhaps it is worth while repeating them to show how many government agencies are working in this field of research, analysis, examination and reporting on energy matters. There is the dominion coal board; the atomic energy control board; the international joint commission; the water resources branch of the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources; the interdepartmental committee on energy; and the national research council. The danger of duplication and overlapping, confusion and conflict is obvious.
Now may I say a word about the regulatory functions of the proposed board, which is something we will be discussing in much greater detail when we are in committee. Those functions are limited in the present bill, at least at the moment, to the licensing of construction and operation of international power lines, export of power, construction and operation of interprovincial and international

National Energy Board oil and gas pipe lines, the import and export of gas, and possibly the export and import of oil.
First, then, may I say a word about the regulatory functions which I have mentioned dealing with power. We on this side agree that these are matters which should be controlled by a public authority. There is not much difference of opinion between us on that score except that we are worried-we will have something to say about this in committee-about the suggestion by the minister that exceptional circumstances may justify the licensing of power exports for a period longer than one year. I am not sure whether he used the period of 25 years or not. The Gordon commission report points out that this might be necessary in changed circumstances, that it might be wise for the government to depart from the policy it has followed for many years of licensing from year to year. I am not taking issue with that in principle, but I do suggest that if this is to be done and these licences are to be extended for a longer period than one year, that should be done through parliamentary sanction rather than merely by order in council.
Then there is also a danger of duplication and conflict, and indeed confusion, in this question of control of the export of power. The minister knows perfectly well, of course, that the Canadian section of the international joint commission has at the present time the responsibility of studying and making recommendations regarding power projects in boundary waters and other public projects on international rivers which may be referred to the commission by the two governments of the United States and Canada. But under this proposed bill which is now before us, every project of this kind approved by the international joint commission and involving the construction of international power lines or the export of power will have to be reviewed and approved as well by the national energy board, and surely there is a danger of conflict there. Also under the International River Improvements Act which was passed in 1955 the same possibility of conflict and confusion arises between the licence which is required from the department concerned under that act and the obligation of the new board to review and consent to these matters. I believe that it would have been possible to have avoided these dangers of overlapping and confusion through a better allocation and integration of functions between the various governmental agencies concerned.
Then there is a third subject, the construction of gas pipe lines and the import and export of gas. We believe that it is right that natural gas service and its development

as a public utility should be under government regulation. But we also believe that these regulations should be of a type and administered in such a way that will not encourage inefficiency. Under this bill export sales of gas will be contingent now upon approval by the provincial authorities, the national energy board, the governor in council, and the federal power commission of the United States. In the case of domestic and export long term contracts, you will have to deal with proven suppliers at one end and an established and responsible distributor at the other. We know that local franchises are involved, and political considerations, sometimes indefensible ones, arise at various levels of government, and we also know that profiteering can take place. Delay and disappointment are inevitable. That means that most promotions in this field require hearings, negotiations, interventions, reassessment of positions, all of which take a long time, and these delays add to costs. Where a project is finally approved, the ultimate terms and conditions often reduce its profitability far below earlier expectations. Therefore while we do agree, Mr. Speaker, that this field must be subject to public regulation, in the public interest the administrative set-up and the procedures designed for that purpose should be efficient, and should minimize delays and difficulties. Perhaps the government will be able to convince us that the machinery established in this bill for this purpose is the most effective which could have been drawn up.
Now I come to another subject, the export and import of oil. There should be no difficulty about the export of oil because I think we are all agreed that any interference by government in the export of oil should be reduced to a minimum, because it is of first importance to encourage in every way possible the export of our oil into United States markets, especially now when it is going to be a little easier than it would have been perhaps a month ago. But the import of oil is a different thing, and it is this aspect of the bill to which we take the greatest exception. On Friday last the minister said, and I quote from his statement as reported at page 3930 of Hansard:
There is no requirement of national policy to be served at present by licensing the import of oil.
And, again, he said:
It would seem unwise at the present moment to take any action by way of import control which might give rise to misunderstanding and possibly call the arrangement into question.
The arrangement he had in mind was the arrangement recently made with the United States. Then the minister added:

It would be premature to do so until the second report of the Borden commission in respect of this matter has been received and considered.
We share these views as to the undesirability of acting, even through parliament, at this time with regard to this matter, but what is the government doing now in this bill? In clause 87, in spite of the words of the minister that there is no necessity for action at this time, the government is asking for power by order in council to take action which, it says, is not necessary now and may not be necessary in the future. That power it to be used against one commercial import singled out from thousands of others, and a very important commercial import at that. And this power is not power to act through parliament, but power for the government to act by order in council and without any consideration of an emergency to justify this power being used, or the action taken. That is an astonishing request to be made of this house by a government which consists of members most of whom had some very strong words to use about this kind of thing a few years ago. What a betrayal of all the brave, emotional words used by members of the Conservative party during the debate on the Defence Production Act in 1955. Where are the memories of the impassioned appeals to the rights and privileges of parliament of those days? Have they so soon been forgotten? Where are the Pyms and Hampdens, the parliamentary flag wavers and flag wearers of those days?

speechtext: I am glad you recognized we were advocating freedom then.

speechtext:
I am trying to show the minister the great departure there has been as evidenced in this action now, from the words used in those days; and this departure throws a very lurid light on the meaning of the words which were used at that time.
The excuse now is merely that things may have to be done in an emergency in order to deal with oil imports. That is the excuse given by the minister, that we might have to act quickly. But is the security of the nation at stake in this issue? Would there be no time to consult parliament in a matter of this kind? This, apparently, is the minister's argument, that there would be no time to consult parliament because it might be necessary to act quickly. That is what the Minister of Trade and Commerce stated, and I quote the words he used last Friday:
If the need arose it would in all probability arise quickly, and would require quick action to avert serious disruption. For this reason it is proposed to make the power applicable by proclamation.
But when the minister of trade and commerce a few years ago asked for discretionary power of this kind to be used in a national
National Energy Board emergency only and not merely to deal with the import of a commodity, this is what the same hon. gentleman had to say about the minister of trade and commerce of that day, Mr. C. D. Howe:
He has appeared to prefer to do things quickly rather than by the slower methods of parliament.
That was the statement which the present Minister of Trade and Commerce made on June 13, 1955, as reported at page 4688 of Hansard.
And the Minister without Portfolio from Toronto (Mr. Macdonnell), the hon. member for Greenwood, had this to say in the same debate, and I wish he was in his seat tonight to hear me repeat these words. At that time, when the request was made for this power under order in council to deal, not with the import of a commodity but with a national emergency, these were the words he used:
This is arbitrary power. This is the antithesis of our way of life. This is the antithesis of the rule of law, described by Dicey when he says that wide arbitrary powers are the absolute antithesis.
I wonder whether, if the hon. gentleman were in his seat tonight, he could defend this particular provision? I wonder if he would vote for it? I wonder if he would give the sanction of his parliamentary prestige and purity to it?
And then there was the Minister of Justice (Mr. Fulton). I regret having to read these quotations in the absence of the ministers concerned, but in this same debate when the government of that day was asking for power by order in council, that hon. gentleman quoted these words with ardent approval from a British pamphlet, as reported on page 4732 for June 13.
Those who give and those who receive arbitrary power are alike criminal and there is no man but is bound to resist it to the best of his power, whenever it shall show its face in the world. It is a crime to bear it when it can be rationally shaken off. ... Law and arbitrary power are in dreadful enmity.
Of course, the present Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) took part in this debate, and he was naturally even more emotional for the time being than any of the others. On June 28, 1955, as reported at page 5385 of Hansard, dealing with the request by the government of that day for power by order in council to deal with a national emergency, he had this to say:
Parliament! What is parliament to the minister? Parliament is not even to be permitted to be a partner with this all-powerful government in working out this program of defence production. Bring these matters to parliament? Why, the idea is unthinkable to this government opposite. What is parliament, anyway? Parliament to them is but a nuisance. We have had proof abundant today, sir;

National Energy Board all this talk, all this poppycock about parliament is just lip service from this all-powerful government opposite.
However, it was the Minister of Trade and Commerce himself who put the matter best when he said, as reported at page 4688 and 4689:
Normally ministers come to parliament and ask for extension of their powers or for special powers for special purposes and parliament examines the situation, makes the grant of power and withdraws it when the crisis has subsided.
And then he went on:
There are no angels in the House of Commons, and precautions are necessary when we are entrusting the government of men to men.
There are no angels in the House of Commons today, especially on the government benches. The argument which the minister made at that time in respect of an application of powers to be used by order in council in respect of a national emergency surely applies one hundredfold to an application in this bill for power by order in council merely to deal with the import of a commercial commodity.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext: Would the Leader of the Opposition permit a question? Has he not overlooked the fact that the debate on the Defence Production Act in 1955 hinged on the request of the government of that day to give those powers to the minister of trade and commerce in perpetuity? It was that to which we objected, and we said: come back to parliament every two years.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, these were
powers to be used only in case of national emergency, and the minister must know that the bill as passed did not give the minister power in perpetuity; it gave the minister power for five years. The five-year period lapses, I may add, if the minister has forgotten, in a couple of weeks. But the minister's excuse is that we have to act quickly, never mind parliament, we have to act quickly in case we have to put restrictions on the import of oil. I cannot understand why there is this necessity for haste in the case of oil. Is it a question of defence and security, or oil sanctions, or something like that? These are some aspects of this bill, Mr. Speaker, which cause us anxiety on this side, and which we will deal with in more detail when we get to the committee stage.
I have already said that we would support the principle of the bill because we are in favour of the establishment of a national energy board; but I repeat that there are a good many features of this bill which we do not like and which we will do our best to get changed in the committee stage. We

are not satisfied, as I have said, with the administrative set-up and the allocation of functions envisaged in this bill. We are convinced that the proposed arrangements will lead to duplication and possible conflict between the new board and other related existing government agencies. We think that in this bill-notwithstanding what the minister said about it on Friday and earlier-the government has failed to guard adequately against those dangers. We think it should have proposed at least a re-allocation of functions of some of those agencies, and indeed it might have brought some of those agencies under this board or under a single government department.
But while there is this danger of duplication on the administrative level there is also an important gap. There is no provision for consultation and liaison between the United States and Canada, and more particularly between the federal power commission and the national energy board. I know the minister discussed this the other night and he indicated why the government found it necessary to reject some of the recommendations of the Borden commission on this matter; but he did say that they were trying to work out satisfactory arrangements for liaison with the United States authorities. However, the minister must know that in most cases where those two agencies will be involved, the United States commission will have to issue an import permit-I am looking at it from the Canadian point of view-and the Canadian board will have to issue an export permit. The United States board and the Canadian board, I should think, would be bound, unless great care were exercised, to use different criteria. If there is no basic arrangement between the two countries, the applicants may have to travel between Washington and Ottawa without making very much progress, and perhaps for a very long time. In my view at least, that is likely to happen, and it would be most undesirable.
I do suggest to the minister, though I know he tried to deal with this the other night, that some basic arrangement in this field of energy between the two governments may well be required and be required quickly. Perhaps the precedent of the 1909 treaty on boundary waters may be invoked. Perhaps a similar arrangement may have to be ultimately worked out covering the field of energy between the two countries and providing for some kind of international joint commission in this particular field. I am not suggesting and I am not criticizing the government for not having put that in this bill. I quite realize that it would not be possible but I do suggest that in the working out of this bill

something like that may be found to be necessary. I hope the matter will be given very serious consideration.
While there is in our view duplication and gaps in the administrative arrangements provided by the bill, it seems to us to have an even more serious shortcoming in that it does not provide any national policy or guidance on energy questions.
Before issuing a certificate in respect of a pipe line or an international power line, the proposed board is required to ensure, primarily, that the project is economically feasible. I recognize that the main test to be applied by the board will be-if I read the bill correctly-the protection of the existing facilities and the control of competition. Moreover, the bill provides that the tolls to be determined by the board shall be just and reasonable. There is your criteria, "just and reasonable". Finally, before issuing an export licence, the board must be satisfied that the energy to be exported is in surplus and that the price to be charged is just and reasonable having regard to the public interest.
Those, Mr. Speaker, are the only policy principles contained in this bill and the only guides which are given to the board in carrying out the functions allocated to the board by this bill. Those policies are so vague that they will be of little use to the board in carrying out and discharging its responsibilities. Indeed, the bill does not provide any policy on energy and the board will have to develop such a policy if it wishes to use its powers consistently, according to certain specific principles. That, I say, is a very unsatisfactory state of affairs. The Borden commission, in its recommendations, did have-whether you approve of them or whether you agree with them or not-a national policy in mind when it recommended that the board be required to take into account, and I quote from the recommendation of the commission:
The advisability of encouraging the development in Canada of processing industries relating to energy and sources of energy as distinct from the export of unprocessed natural resources.
In making that recommendation the Borden commission felt that our sources of energy should be used, not only to serve our national development but they also suggested that the board concern itself with-and again I quote from the Borden commission recommendation:
Arrangements with respect to disposal of byproducts and avoidance of waste.
I ask the minister whether he can point to anything in the bill that deals with this
National Energy Board matter, a matter which is of very great importance to this industry and to the development of energy. As we all know-some perhaps know it better than I do because they are more familiar with this subject- the sale of such constituents of wet or sour gas as propane and sulphur helps to render fuel operations much more profitable. As our exports of gas to the United States increase- and we all hope they will increase

the disposal of those by-products will become a major problem in Canada. Sulphur, which was in such short supply only a few years ago, as we all know is now in surplus supply. Many of the liquid petroleum gases, including propane, will encounter increasingly difficult marketing problems, and yet they are becoming more and more important to the development of this industry. Were it possible to convert some of these materials into chemical products and to find substantial export markets for those products some of those difficulties might be avoided. The Canadian market is quite limited, and the United States market for chemical products, as we know, is not easily accessible, having regard to tariff barriers. Surely this is one field in which some bargaining with the United States might prove to be highly profitable as they more and more realize they are going to need our surplus, and that is the only kind of gas they are going to get, gas; but there does not seem to us to be any reference to this matter or any recognition of its importance in this particular bill.
Therefore, we contend, Mr. Speaker, that this bill is inadequate in the sense that it does not lay down any national policy for energy development. I think this is a major shortcoming. But whatever we may think of this bill, there is little doubt that it can have far-reaching implications on Canada's future. It is because of our recognition of its importance that we put forward these suggestions for improving it.
If this bill is to be made as effective as it can be made, surely those who have drafted the bill and those who are putting it before parliament now would be glad to submit the bill to experts in the field of energy where it could be scrutinized and where suggestions could be made for its improvement. It is for that reason that we have already made the suggestion, which I repeat with all earnestness, that the bill should be referred by the government to a standing committee so that witnesses can be called, evidence can be given and the bill can perhaps be made more effective.
There are good precedents for this course. There is a good precedent in this present session. The unemployment insurance bill has been referred on the government's own

National Energy Board initiative to the committee on industrial relations and in 1955 a bill on international rivers improvements was referred to the standing committee on external affairs. That action proved to be most useful because several provisions in the bill were altered as a result of the examination given to it by the committee on external affairs.
So, Mr. Speaker, I ask the government if they will consider the reference of a bill of this importance and complexity to a standing committee, whatever standing committee is most suitable, so that evidence can be taken before that standing committee and so that as a result of that evidence and as a result of the examination given to the legislation the bill can be improved and made more effective than we think it is in its present form to reach the objective we all have in mind in setting up a national energy board.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the bill being debated by the house at the present time, has for its purpose the setting up of a national energy board, and in my opinion this is one of the most far-reaching bills that has come before this session or any other session for a long time. I may say that energy is the key to industrial development and national welfare. The people of the west who reside in that tremendous area commonly known as the sedimentary basin are fully aware of the tremendous resources they have in their back yard.
For those of you who are not familiar with the area and its geology from which the oil and gas supply originates, let me say that from the crest of the Rocky mountains stretching eastward almost, through Manitoba and north to the Arctic and into the arctic islands is a tremendous area known as the sedimentary basin, and it is in that area that we find these tremendous deposits of oil and gas. The exploitation of these resources, the finding of markets for the products and the development of petrochemical industries in the west are what we are looking and hoping for.
In order to have sound economic development of these vast resources it was considered necessary in the interests of the people, in the interests of the industry too, may I say, and in the interests of equity within the industry to advance the idea of an energy board. When we are talking about a natural resource like gas we must realize that it is an expendable resource. It is a resource that can be drained off by use and therefore we must give greater consideration to that factor than we would in the case of a replaceable resource such as hydroelectric power, for after all the water keeps flowing over the dams and hydroelectric power is generated, but when you draw gas

and oil from the ground you are draining off a non-replaceable natural resource. That brings up the need for some measure of public control.
I am not one who believes by any means that everything has to be controlled but there are certain things, and gas is one of them, where you have got to have a certain amount of control in the public interest. That was found when the Alberta government set up the conservation board in that province. After the energy board has been set up to look after the interests of Canada with respect to oil, gas and other energy products the same thing will be found to be true.
I rose to speak on this matter because in my constituency in Alberta is found a great share of the natural gas that will warm the homes of Alberta. Turner valley is located there and also Flat Top mountain and Savannah creek. The tremendous gas and oil deposits in the vicinity of Pincher Creek are also located in my constituency. All along the eastern slope of the Rockies there are these tremendous fields of oil and gas. Therefore, with this tremendous surplus of energy we have to look forward to markets and I for one am 100 per cent behind the finding of export markets for these products. I think they have to be exported. Above all, if I am to say anything about export on the floor of the house I wish to say that an energy board should be set up for the purpose of looking after the public interest with respect to export. The question is how the exporting should be done in order to protect the public interest.
Let me call to your attention, Mr. Speaker, some of the factors which I think should be considered by an energy board. Coming from the west as I do and having worked very closely on these matters as a consultant in Calgary for a number of years, I feel I can speak with a certain amount of inward feeling and understanding of some of the economic relationships that pertain to this matter in the west. I should think that some of the factors which will need to be considered are, first, the pools which are to be drained. When we export gas careful consideration should be given as to what pools are drained. We do not want to see a pool drained right beside a great metropolitan centre which is using gas while another pool away off in the hinterland is not drained although there are pipe lines leading to it. Some consideration should be given to the question of what pools are drained when gas is exported.
The second factor is the price to the producers. If we are going to export gas it is necessary to take into account the 600 to

800 capped wells in Alberta where people have put their capital and see that they are given a decent return on this capital they have invested. I for one would like to see these people receive a fair share of the sale price of the gas in the foreign market. It is my thought that through more effective bargaining we should receive the best price possible for the gas we export. I am not so sure that an individual company, interested in completing a deal, is likely to act in the best interests of the public when it comes to agreeing on a price which would be the best price that Canada should obtain in relation to the price which consumers in Canada must pay.
The exporter of natural gas deals in wholesale quantities. In other words, if a gas company is making a deal to sell a tremendous amount of gas they will sell it a little cheaper than if they were selling a small amount. My contention is that we should look at the sale of gas from the retailers' point of view. Out in Alberta, where the climate is cold in winter the individual user of gas will consume perhaps 4 or 5 times as much gas as the consumer in the warmer climate. If we are looking at the problem from the consumer's point of view, then the man in Alberta is the big consumer, not the man in the warmer climate. If the price were established on the basis of the consumer, then that big consumer in Canada should pay a lower price for his gas than the small consumer in a warmer climate. All I am saying is that those who are looking after the public interest should protect the interests of the Canadian consumer by taking this matter into consideration.
If we are to establish industries, and have the industrial development hoped for then natural gas must be sold at a low price and the supply available for a long time. The petrochemical industries in the west are capable of producing in the neighbourhood of 10,000 products. Let us take the plant at Sarnia as an example. There are over 10,000 products that can be produced from oil at that point. The Polymer Corporation alone produces some 600 or 700 different commodities. As you know the gas which comes out of the ground is about 90 per cent wet gas and only 10 per cent methane gas. It is only the methane gas that goes through the pipes and into homes. The so-called wet gas is a sour gas which has to be put through processing plants to strip out the methane, ethane, propane, butane and hydrogen sulphide.
Some fields in the west for instance around Okotoks and in the Pincher Creek area are capable of shipping out a trainload of sulphur per day. There is a tremendous development 66968-9-255
National Energy Board in sulphur production alone, and there are tremendous quantities of propane, butane and ethane, all of which must find markets. When Canada is exporting tremendous quantities of natural gas to the United States it will be done through a pipe that has a 36-inch diameter, flowing 450 million cubic feet per day. This is a tremendous amount of gas and will result in a lot of by-products which will need to find markets either in the United States or through the development of industry in Canada. This is one of the most troublesome aspects of the oil and gas industry in the west, particularly the gas industry. Alberta has a conservation board and it is the policy of that board to require that gas and its by-products be conserved. This has meant pumping certain surplus products back into the ground, and that is being done to a certain extent. A certain amount of propane is flared in the summer. Wherever gas is flared, as was the case in the Turner valley during the early development period the loss to society was tremendous. I think everyone in this dominion frowns on that type of wasteful operation.
Now, coming back to industrial development I should like to say that in the Crowsnest area, for example, where we expect this pipe line will find its way through to markets in the United States, we are tremendously interested in the development of industry. If we are going to develop the iron ore or any of the other minerals in the Crowsnest Pass area, and if you are going to have secondary industries developed, we must have a price for gas which will be in line with the ability of companies to pay and with their ability to attract capital.
There is one other point I should like to mention and that is that those who are charged with the responsibility of examining the contracts of the different companies should look into the question of escalator clauses in those contracts. I am told these gas exporting companies have escalator clauses in their contracts. In other words the price of gas is set at a certain level and then it goes up year after year in increments and gradually the price is increased. I have heard that these escalator clauses are based on economic trends. I would recommend to the government that they look into the question of who drew these economic trends. There is no other industry in this country that I know of that has escalator clauses in contracts relating to the things which it sets out to sell.
Then, having said that, I believe there should be a sufficient margin of profit given to gas exporting companies to enable them

National Energy Board to attract capital and to make their operations profitable. There is no one in the picture who is going to deny them that. What we do want to see is that they act in the public interest. We should maintain equity among the different producers. It is possible that a big company such as Imperial Oil or Shell, with lots of bargaining power, could obtain a better deal than some small Canadian gas company. I believe that the economic forces should be bent in such a way that, over a long period of time, Canadian ownership will develop. Above all, we should maintain equity among the producers of gas and encourage Canadians to assume leadership in the production of gas and oil.
In so far as those of you who are not familiar with the gas and oil industry are concerned, I might say that natural gas often results from the exploration for oil. A company may be drilling for oil, and quite often strike natural gas. The valuation of gas or oil is a problem worthy of mention. Let me say for the benefit of hon. members who are unfamiliar with the oil and gas industry that if we are looking at the mathematics of investment, it depends on how fast you can exploit the supply in the well and this in turn depends on how much the conservation board will allow you to sell. That plus an assumed discount rate determines the price of the well. Any income from gas beyond 25 or 30 years, if discounted to the present, assuming an interest rate, does not amount to much. That is one reason why we have had a tremendous campaign to influence the public that we ought to cut and get out of gas in 25 years.
I do not blame that one body of people who are concerned with the exporting of gas, namely the pipe line companies. Their interests are to get their money out as quickly as possible; that is only good business; that is only natural. What I am trying to get at is that there is a conflict between that speed with which the export companies wish to get their capital back out and the public interest. The other side of the picture is the investment of capital in secondary industries. If you are going to put money into a petrochemical industry that will cost several millions of dollars, the very first question the investor is going to ask is this: How long is my source of raw material going to last?
It has been my humble duty to run an economic consulting business at Calgary for western Canada. Many companies have come to me and asked me for a study of where they should locate in Alberta. After you have gone through all the different factors necessary to consider in evaluating the potential income of that particular company, you


will come to the conclusion that much depends upon the cost and continuity of the source of hydrocarbons. If you can show, as in the Medicine Hat area, where you have a source of gas that will probably last for 75 years and more and the cost is likely to be relatively cheap, that is where the industry is located. So when it comes to the investing of capital, there is that principle to which investors pay attention, namely how long is my source of hydrocarbons going to last. But that consideration is in conflict with the speed at which exporting companies wish to get their money back out of gas fields once developed.
The setting up of a national energy board is a step taken primarily for western Canada. These tremendous deposits of oil and gas and energy are largely located in western Canada. Since they are located out west, this board should have on it personnel who understand the problems of western Canada. I have watched the debate on this energy bill in this house and I have noticed that the people of Ontario are only mildly interested. I can understand why that should be so. We in western Canada are primarily concerned. It is us who should be considered when choosing people to be on the board. British Columbia, Alberta, Saskatchewan and to some extent Manitoba-yes, and Ontario-are the provinces concerned. But as to eastern Canada, what is the use in having on the board somebody from Halifax who knows very little about the energy resources in western Canada? All I am saying is this. They are good people and everything else, but this particular piece of legislation is largely for western Canada and I should hope that those who are in eastern Canada would look upon it as such and that they, for once at any rate, would regard us in the west as grown-up children and give us an opportunity really to direct this particular board in the interests of developing our tremendous resources out there, getting the capital and getting these petrochemical industries and other industries established.
I now want to say a few words on another matter. I have been tremendously impressed by the words of the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) and of other members of the opposition and of the C.C.F. They have gone to great lengths in praising the report of the Gordon royal commission which recommended the establishment of an energy board. The Gordon royal commission made the energy board their number one recommendation. You may be interested in knowing how that recommendation got into the report.
Mr. Gordon set up a system and asked for the help across Canada of scientists, economists and everyone whose services he

could draw upon. In Alberta he asked the Alberta government to prepare a brief for the information of the Gordon royal commission. I was asked by the Alberta government to head the preparation of the Alberta brief. We made the creation of a national energy board our number one recommendation. Through Dr. Stewart who was on the royal commission with whom I talked many times and Mr. Gordon himself and others, as a result of the way in which they were impressed with the soundness of the recommendation and I may say the brief is in print for anyone who wishes to read it, the question of an energy board found its way into the final report of the Gordon royal commission.
Let me go back one step further because I want to give credit to the people who deserve credit. I was asked to take leadership and prepare "Alberta's Economic Prospects" which was Alberta's brief to the Gordon royal commission. There were some 50 people who made submissions to that brief. Each department of the government and the university, the research council, the power commission and many others were assigned by me to prepare certain submissions. An outline was prepared first and the submission written. The paper was then read by me and others and criticized. A series of teams prepared the various submissions and I acted as the economist with each team and co-ordinated the final paper. This was known as "Alberta's Economic Prospects" to the Gordon royal commission. During this work I made an assignment on coal to Mr. Lang of the research council. When he had his submission prepared and I read it I found that over a few pages from the beginning he had recommended an energy board but he had stricken it out. He thought that it should not be up to him to recommend an energy board. I said, "I think we ought to take that particular feature out of there and play it up and hold some meetings". So we called a meeting over in the office of the minister of economic affairs. Mr. Lang and Dr. Grace were assigned the task of redrafting the recommendation for the establishment of an energy board. That was done and we worked it over again, and from there it was made number one recommendation in "Alberta's Economic Prospects". You will find it in the back of the printed publication. This report was prepared back in October of 1955. Although the matter of an energy board had been mentioned by others this action in Alberta's brief focused attention on it. I do not wish to take any credit for it. I want to see all of the credit go to Mr. Lang of the research council of Alberta, Dr. Grace and others who worked with him. They are the people who deserve the credit.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was very interested to note that the last speaker referred to this bill, like some of the other bills we have dealt with this session, as a bill concerning mainly his province or the other western provinces of Canada. However, that is not what the bill says. This is a national energy bill, and there are
101	clauses. I would assume that out of the 101 clauses some of them must, or should, apply to the people who live in the other parts of Canada.
We listened very closely to what the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) said tonight. He said many things about this particular bill. In fact, much of what he said reminded me of Shakespeare's "Much Ado About Nothing", and I think that is about what the situation was. The member who has just sat down also referred to this bill as a far-reaching bill. It is far-reaching all right; it goes everywhere and gets nowhere.
This particular bill, in my opinion, is one of the most important bills which has been considered for a long time. I think that one of the oversights in this bill is the fact that it is called a national energy bill when in fact it is not. I think this bill is a bastardization of a great number of bills which we have at the present time, including our export and import bills concerning the production and sale of gas. This bill does not talk about matters of energy which should be in an energy bill, but which are completely neglected. A national energy bill should contain legislation which will govern gas, oil, coal and hydro power. Atomic energy must be taken into consideration also in a national energy bill. These things have not been taken into consideration.
This bill was no doubt prompted by the discussions spearheaded by the decision made by the previous government, and particularly by the then minister of trade and commerce. This bill in the main considers the matter which was raised by the trans-Canada pipe

National Energy Board line. Even in this field where the Conservative government conducted an election on this particular issue, and beat the drums across the country on the issue of the trans-Canada pipe line and the faults and manipulations which took place in the introduction of that pipe line, the government has completely neglected the responsibilities which they said they would assume in that particular field.
They have failed in the main to mention the other fields of national energy. The 101 clauses in this particular bill do not even consider the major sources of energy which we are going to use for many years to come. There is nothing in this bill that concerns our greatest potential energy in future years, the matter of atomic energy. That has not been considered. Therefore I would agree that this bill is far-reaching; it goes to many places but really does not get any place at all.
I suggest that this bill could be supported quite well by the Liberal party, and I was not surprised when the Leader of the Opposition rose and said that he was willing to support it in principle. I would like to know where he finds the principle in this bill. This is a conglomeration of a number of other bills and there is no principle in it. If the Leader of the Opposition does not know there is no principle in it, then I think it is an excuse for the attitude taken in the past on this matter of national energy, and in particular the manipulation and handling of the trans-Canada pipe line.
I think particularly in the last few years it has generally been decided that national energy is something which belongs to the Canadian people and should be used for the Canadian people. One of our greatest natural resources in years gone by has been hydro. I can think of one or two isolated cases in the province of Ontario where we have not nationalized hydro. I am thinking of a particular case not too far away from the constituency of the Leader of the Opposition. Perhaps it is something he could give some consideration to, because he represents a riding that is affected by a particular company. In Sault Ste. Marie they still have the natural resource of hydro controlled by a private company. I am thinking of people who live in the village of Searchmont which is only 10 or 12 miles from a major transmission line of this particular company, but there is no electricity in that community. They have built one of the most modern sawmills in Ontario, probably one of the most modern in Canada today. They have built this sawmill but have had to put in their own power development in the sawmill for the simple reason that private industry, as always, fails to serve the needs of the

people when dealing with a national commodity, and certainly hydro power comes under that category.
We have seen also abuses over the years of these commodities and groups of commodities which have been nationalized. I am thinking again of the Ontario hydro as it affects a certain community not too far from my area. I pay five cents for the first quota of hydro power in rural electrification in northern Ontario, while at the same time the people of Quebec are buying the product of the Ontario hydro at half a cent a kilowatt and selling it to their own people through a co-operative in the province of Quebec at three-quarters of a cent. So even where we have nationalized some of these industries on a provincial or municipal basis, sometimes we find they do not serve the needs of the people because the people who implement them fail to make them work for the benefit of the people.
This government has failed miserably to do anything about many of the major sources of national energy. I do not really see why they set up the Borden commission to do a survey of national energy in Canada. I have read parts of their report and they have proved of great interest. I think the report has been well prepared and should serve the government in developing a national policy. But has the government taken any of the recommendations of the commission into consideration? Two of the major recommendations were, first, that there should be compulsion in the selling rates, so the government ignored that; and another recommendation was that the tolls, rates and tariffs should be calculated to yield a fair rate of return on the shareholders' equity. This recommendation was also ignored because it interferes with private enterprise. The government does not want them to get a fair return; they want them to get an exorbitant return.
It is apparently the hope that if this money is piled high enough, if the graft and profiteering which is taken out of the distribution of national energy in particular can be piled high enough, few of the crumbs may spill and fall on the floor where the multitude can share in some small way in those profits. We do not really care about the size of the profits which are being piled up as long as a few crumbs fall off and the ordinary people get their share of the crumbs.
Another question which we must take into consideration when discussing the establishment of a national energy board is coal. For years we have depended on coal, and we have on the statute books an agglomeration of many acts which deal with that industry. We

subsidize coal production in two or three different ways; we assist in the digging of it, in the shipping of it and in the selling of it. This is a commodity which could certainly be used for the betterment of all Canadians if it were brought under a national plan which would utilize it for the good of all the people.
One of the things we must keep in mind is that national energy represents one of the greatest resources we have in the country. We, in Ontario, have nationalized our hydro industry but we have also abused it badly. We have abused it to the extent that there are only a few more developments which can take place in the province which could be of benefit to the people generally. We have not carried out this operation on a planned basis. We have considered how it was likely to affect private profits rather than how it could best contribute to the development of Canada. We have given much more consideration to how this development was going to help the profiteers than how it would assist the mass of the people of this country. We have kept the requirements of the financial institutions more in mind than the need to develop our resources for the good of all.
If we lose our national resources, it should be remembered that there is nothing which can be put in their place, and this should make us particularly careful and responsible in our approach, especially to those areas which are so far untapped and undeveloped. If the government is sincere in wishing to develop those areas which up to the present have not been developed, one of the most effective ways of doing this would be to control our national energy and supply energy at a low rate of cost to communities where natural resources are lacking. We should find that a little subsidization in the field of the development of natural energy would be a lot more profitable than a great deal of subsidization in fields which are much less productive-the development of secondary industries, for example.
The government appointed the Borden commission to make this investigation. I wonder just why these commissions are set up, and I think the Canadian people are beginning to ask themselves the same question. I say this because after the Borden commission has been set up by the government, the government declared that no matter what recommendations the commission brought in it did not intend to pay any attention to them. The question arises: why set these commissions up at all? Do we need to stall for time until some decision can be reached? Did we ask these intelligent and highly reputed gentlemen to travel across this country, to interview
National Energy Board people, to examine the situation in all parts of Canada and to hear representations from the major organizations just in order to give the government some measure of time in which they can overcome a growing understanding on the part of the Canadian people with regard to the place of natural gas in a national energy scheme?
Did the government want to overcome the feeling which is developing across the country that Canada has been sold down the river by the privateers and profiteers? Did the government want to let the smoke of that battle -the battle which they helped to lead-die down so that they could do exactly as the former government did, and bring in a bill which does nothing to assist the planning or development of Canadian resources and which does absolutely nothing to develop our sources and supply of natural energy for the good of the Canadian people? I think the Canadian people are going to ask why the Borden commission was set up. Obviously it was not set up to tell the government anything, because the government has completely ignored it. The government has paid no attention to its views.

FROZEN SHRIMP IMPORTS FROM CHINA
speechtext:
1.	Has any frozen shrimp been imported from China to Canada during (a) 1958; (b) 1959?
2.	If so, at what ports were they landed, on what dates, what quantites, dollar value, and who were the Canadian importers?
Answer by: Hon. Gordon Churchill (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
1.	Statistics are not available on the imports of frozen shrimps as they are not recorded separately.
2.	As above.
